title: Residential fees for a foreign person

sections.heading: When to pay a fee
sections.text:
If you are a foreign person investing in residential property in Australia, you must pay a fee when:

- applying for approval to purchase a residential property or for an exemption certificate
- applying to vary (make changes to) your existing approval
- lodging your vacancy fee return – if a fee is payable.

There are very limited circumstances where we grant a fee waiver or remission.

sections.heading: How much is the fee
sections.text:
Your application fee is generally based on the value of the property you intend to buy.

Fees for property developers applying for a *New or near-new dwelling exemption certificate* are different to residential property application fees.

sections.heading: Types of residential fees > Variation application fees
sections.text:
You must pay a fee to apply to vary an existing foreign investment approval.

For 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, the fee is:

- $4,600 for a simple variation (considered immaterial or minor)
- $31,300 for a complex variation (not of an immaterial or minor nature).

We will cap your fee where you are seeking to vary an application notice and you originally paid a lower fee. For example, if you requested a complex variation in November 2026 for an approval where you originally paid a $15,100 fee, the variation fee is capped at $15,100.

sections.heading: Types of residential fees > Tenants in common share of fees
sections.text: If you are purchasing the property as tenants in common, the fee payable for the interest is equal to your percentage of ownership in the property.

sections.heading: Types of residential fees > Tenants in common share of fees > Example: tenants in common
sections.text:
Sara is a foreign person, and she is purchasing a new dwelling with another investor as tenants in common.

On 1 August 2026, she applies for residential approval to purchase 25% of a $1.5 million property with the other investor.

The application fee for a $1.5 million property is $31,300. When Sara submits her application, she needs to pay $7,825 which is 25% of the total fee for the property.

End of example

sections.heading: Annual vacancy fee
sections.text:
You pay a vacancy fee if:

- your property is vacant for 183 days (6 months) or more in a vacancy year
- you fail to lodge your annual vacancy fee return on time.

For vacancy years starting 9 April 2024 the fee will be double your foreign investment application fee.

Fees are calculated when you lodge your vacancy fee return.

sections.heading: Annual vacancy fee > Example: working out your vacancy fee
sections.text:
Rishi is a foreign person looking to buy a newly developed apartment in the Sydney area for under $2 million. He applies for approval for a residential property exemption certificate for a new property in September 2026 and pays the $31,300 application fee.

Rishi's application is approved, and he has 12 months to purchase a newly developed apartment. On 2 November 2026 he completes settlement on a newly developed apartment and makes it available for rent.

Rishi's vacancy year will end on 1 November each year. He will need to lodge a vacancy fee return by 1 December 2027. If the apartment was unoccupied and not available to rent for more than 183 days (6 months), he will pay a vacancy fee of $62,600. This is twice the fee he paid for the exemption certificate application.

End of example

sections.heading: Application fee for property developers
sections.text:
Property developers applying for a New or near-new dwelling exemption certificate must pay an initial application fee of $67,400 for applications submitted between 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027.

As a developer you are then required to report the sales of new or near-new dwellings every 6 months. A **separate fee per sale** will be payable for each dwelling sold to a foreign person under the certificate.

sections.heading: Fees are updated once a year
sections.text:
Fees for foreign investment applications are indexed each financial year on 1 July. The information on this page is correct at the time of publishing.

For more information, see The Treasury's Guidance Note 10: Fees.
